yoriki.def: A samurai officer serving under a magistrate, over the constables.

yoshizu.def: Reed blinds: screens woven from cut reed, one product of a reed bed's winter harvest along with thatch.

yosui.def: An irrigation canal - a district's main supply channel, which forks downstream into the ditches that water the fields.

yulin wei.def: The small islet-like polders packed into a water net, named for the irregular overlapping outlines they show from the air.

zaimokuya.def: A timber dealer, whose stacked timber and floated logs need an open yard with a landing on the water at the edge of town.

zaofang.def: The Chinese brewery: the vat hall and yard where grain liquor was made.

zhalan.def: The palings that closed each street of Qing Beijing at night against thieves.

zhang.def: A Chinese length of about 3.3 meters, ten chi.

zokibayashi.def: A worked scrub wood of mixed broadleaf trees regrowing from the stump and cut for fuel; on a new-field household's strip, the wood at its far end kept for that household's own fuel.

zonation.def: The banding of plants around still water, each band on the depth it can stand.

zooplankton.def: The animal half of plankton: minute drifting animals that feed on algae and bacteria and are in turn eaten by the fish.

zuku.def: Pig iron, the tatara's high-carbon product, refined at a separate forge.

ōkaji.def: The refining forge: the second stage of Japanese iron making, which turns the tatara's pig iron and low-carbon fractions into flat bars of forgeable iron. The okajiba is its building.

umayado.def: a Japanese inn that took a traveling guest's own horse into its keeping, or an inn with the stabling to do so; the one picture the record has of such an inn puts the lodging in front and a large stable behind

wagon inn.def: The north-Chinese roadside inn for carters and their animals: simple board and lodging at low cost on a main thoroughfare or in the belt around a city's outskirts, with open ground in the back yard for parking the carts, a long stable with a feeding trough and a tying rail, a grooms' lean-to and a well in the yard.

Tokaido.def: The great highway along Japan's east coast between the shogun's capital and Kyoto, its post towns - Okabe among them - strung with inns, transport offices and relay horses.

knob.def: A setting the map varies from settlement to settlement: where the research supports more than one form, the map rolls between them from its own seed instead of the record choosing one for every map.

Taisho.def: The Japanese era between Meiji and Showa, 1912 to 1926 - modern Japan, by which time the railway had begun displacing packhorse traffic.

ghat.def: A flight of stone steps down a riverbank to the water, used for landing boats, washing and drawing water - and at Varanasi for cremation.

han.def: A daimyo's domain under the Tokugawa shogunate: the territory, and the lord's house and government that held it.

yacheng.def: The innermost walled ring of a Chinese prefectural seat, holding the government offices - the administrative city inside the inner city.

zicheng.def: The inner walled city of a Chinese prefectural seat, standing between the offices' own ring and the outer city.

luocheng.def: The outer city wall of a Chinese walled city, enclosing the residential and commercial quarters around the inner city.

yicheng.def: A wing wall: an extra ring some Chinese cities threw around a suburb that had grown beyond the outer wall, as at Quanzhou.

rinkaku.def: A castle plan whose baileys ring the main bailey on every side, one enclosure inside the next.

renkaku.def: A castle plan whose baileys stand in a row, one beside the next along a ridge or a riverbank.

teikaku.def: A castle plan whose main bailey stands at one edge, against a cliff, a river or the sea, with the other baileys spread on the open side.

light bamboo.def: The lighter of the two bamboo rods of Chinese legal flogging; a sentence of blows with it was the mildest punishment the codes set.

xiang.def: An administrative ward of a Chinese city, the unit into which the settled ground inside and outside the wall was divided.

mitochigai.def: A moat stepped by weirs into pools at different levels, so that its water does not stand as one sheet.

jo.def: A Japanese unit of length of ten shaku, about 3 meters (10 feet); as the suffix -jo on a place name it means castle.

fu.def: In the Rites of Zhou, a square of land a hundred paces on a side, the module by which the classical capital's court and market are each sized.

ake-mutsu.def: The sixth hour of dawn in the Edo reckoning, about 6 in the morning, when a town's gates and wickets opened.

kure-mutsu.def: The sixth hour of dusk in the Edo reckoning, about 6 in the evening, when a town's gates and wickets closed.

tread.def: The worn surface of a way: the strip a road, street, lane or alley is actually walked and carted on.

verge.def: The strip at a road's edge, beside the tread but not on it, where a notice board or a boundary stone stands.

tier.def: One rung of the ladder of settlement sizes these maps draw - hamlet, village, town, provincial city, capital - each at its own scale and densities.

the pool.def: The set of settlement maps this project has drawn and keeps as its worked exhibits; a tolerance or a figure is calibrated against them.

apron.def: The open worked ground in front of a shed or forge: room to lead a horse in and turn it, or to stand fresh charcoal out to cool.

fines.def: The dust and small broken pieces of charcoal; packed tight they hold the heat of their own slow burning, which is what sets a fresh heap alight.

fire gap.def: The clear ground kept between a fire and what would burn: about 6 ft at an attended forge, 30 ft around an unattended charcoal stack, 60 ft around a kiln body.

hoarding.def: A plank screen or fence around a working ground; the county execution ground is drawn without one.

farrier.def: The smith who shoes horses and oxen and trims their hooves; on these maps a trade of the gate caravan yard and the Imperial-road relay town.

throwing.def: Shaping a pot on the wheel - one of the stages, with digging, weathering, drying and firing, that a kiln works gathers on one spot.

weathering.def: Leaving dug clay lying in the open to break down before it is worked.

Danzaemon.def: The hereditary head of the eta of eastern Japan under the shogunate; his Asakusa compound held his residences, storehouses, a shrine, a courtroom and a jail.

chori.def: The head of an outcast community, who guarded it and was paid by its residents; the shogunate ruled the eta and hinin through the chori heads.

Yoshiwara.def: Edo's licensed pleasure quarter, moved in 1656 to Nihon-zutsumi behind Senso-ji, in the city's northeast.

kebiishi.def: The capital's police and judicial office, under which the hinin did the cleaning and the executioner's work.

alternate attendance.def: The shogunate's requirement that a domain lord spend alternate years in Edo, which is why every daimyo kept upper, middle and lower residences there.

Sphere.def: The humanitarian minimum-standards handbook whose water figures - about 400 users to one open well - the record reads backward from.

Song Yingxing.def: The author of the Tiangong Kaiwu of 1637, the illustrated Chinese treatise on crafts and industry this record quotes for the fining hearth.

petuntse.def: Porcelain stone: the crushed rock that, with white clay, makes a Chinese porcelain body.

jagama.def: A snake kiln: the very long single-chamber tunnel kiln of the anagama family.

ō-aza.def: The largest division of a modern Japanese municipality, each answering to one of the old villages it was made from.

shizai.def: The death-penalty class of Edo sentence.

reducing firing.def: Firing with the kiln's air choked, so the starved flame pulls oxygen out of the clay and turns the ware gray.

ablution well.def: The well kept beside a shrine or temple hall for the washing of hands and mouth before worship.

warren.def: The dense block of small commoner dwellings behind the street frontage, packed tight and threaded only by footpaths.

cooper.def: A craftsman who makes barrels, tubs and buckets from wooden staves.

hot-shoeing.def: Shaping the shoe hot at the forge and fitting it to the hoof, as against nailing on a ready-made one.

isohyet.def: A line on a map joining places of equal rainfall; an isotherm joins places of equal temperature.

Sue ware.def: The gray stoneware of ancient Japan, fired hard in a reducing kiln from the fifth century on; the ware of the Nara-period tile-and-pottery kilns.

gassho.def: The steep thatched farmhouse roof of the Sho river valleys, whose king-post-free loft of two to four levels held the household's silkworms as well as keeping the snow off.

king post.def: The upright timber from a tie beam to the ridge of a roof; a roof framed without one leaves its loft clear.

burgage plot.def: The long narrow house plot of an English planned village or town, its short end on the street and a back lane at the far end.

abreuvoir.def: A watering trough or basin at a settlement's water point, used by humans as well as by beasts.

Khitan.def: The horse-riding people of the Liao empire on the Northern Song's frontier, whose cavalry the Hebei pond-and-marsh belt was built against.

superelevation.def: The rise of the water surface on the outside of a bend, which can carry a fast flow over the bank.

backwater.def: The stretch of raised water surface upstream of a weir or a gate; it reaches back a finite distance and then returns to the channel's own depth.

fit zoom.def: The whole map shown at once on the screen - the view a reader opens the page in, as against a zoomed-in one.

kuri.def: The building of a Japanese Buddhist temple that holds its kitchen and, in ordinary usage, the quarters where its monks live; at a village temple, the priest's house.

honden.def: The sanctuary of a Shinto shrine, the small closed building where the deity's object is kept; worshippers stand before it, never in it.

bettō.def: Before 1868, the Buddhist monk who headed the temple attached to a shrine and performed the shrine's rites in Buddhist form.

jingūji.def: A temple attached to a Shinto shrine in the centuries when kami and Buddhas were worshipped together, staffed by monks who served the shrine; almost all were closed or demolished after 1868.

shasō.def: A "shrine monk": the Buddhist monk of a jingūji who was at once the shrine's priest, before 1868.

miyaza.def: The closed association of village households that ran a village shrine's rites, its members serving as priest by yearly turn where the shrine had none.

jochi.def: Land the Edo authorities exempted from the annual tax - temple and shrine precincts and holdings with a document of exemption - outside the vermilion- and black-seal grants.

shuinchi.def: Temple or shrine land confirmed by a shogunal vermilion-seal document (or a daimyo's black seal), tax-free and ranging from thousands of koku down to one.

temizuya.def: The basin or well beside a shrine's approach where a visitor rinses hands and mouth before going on.

tamagaki.def: A shrine's fence - at an ordinary shrine a low fence around the sanctuary alone, often a later donation; at a great shrine, rings of them.

Bishamon.def: The Fortune of Strength, whom warriors swear their vows to; in Japan Bishamonten, an armored guardian deity so bound to the tiger that his shrine sets a pair of stone tigers at its entrance in place of the usual lion-dogs.

votive plaque.def: A small wooden tablet a worshipper leaves at a shrine, carrying a wish or thanks and painted with the deity's emblem - a tiger at a shrine of Bishamon.

lion-dog.def: One of the pair of stone guardian beasts, komainu, set at a shrine's entrance; a shrine of Bishamon sets tigers in their place.

terauke.def: The Edo-period requirement that every household be certified by a Buddhist temple, which issued the papers a person needed to travel or move.

fuse.def: The offering a parish household pays its temple for rites - a gift in name, a fee in practice.

lijia.def: The Ming and Qing system that grouped households by the hundred for tax and corvée; where a Chinese village's population was registered.

Kaie-ji.def: A Zen temple in Sakai whose early-Edo main hall and priest's quarters are one building - the one measured example of a hall and dwelling under one roof.

kami.def: A god of the Japanese tradition - the spirit of a place, a natural force or an ancestor - housed in a shrine's sanctuary. Before 1868 the kami were served together with the Buddhas, at the same sites and by the same monks.

parish.def: The households registered with one Buddhist temple, which buries their dead, conducts their memorials and is supported by their offerings; every household belonged to one.

bay.def: The span between two posts of a building, about one ken (1.8 m); a Japanese building's size is given as so many bays along the ridge by so many across the beams.

ridge span.def: The two plan dimensions of a Japanese building: its length along the line of the roof's ridge, normally the front, and its depth across the beams that run the other way.

honmune-zukuri.def: A regional Japanese farmhouse form with a heavy decorated ridge; a temple dwelling built this way is a farmhouse in all but name.

fire-water.def: Water kept standing beside a wooden building against fire - a barrel, tub or small pond within reach of the eaves.

morijio.def: Small heaps of salt set at a doorway or gate - a Japanese custom of purification and of welcoming good fortune.

nakamon.def: The middle gate: the inner gate of a compound, opening from its outer court into its inner one.

patrol strip.def: The clear walkway kept along the inside of a rampart so guards can pass along the wall.

muster perimeter.def: The boundary of the ground where troops form up; nothing physical marks it, so the map draws it as a dashed line.

precinct.def: The walled grounds of a temple or shrine taken together: its halls, gates, courtyards and garden.

Six Ministries.def: The six departments of government in this setting - Rites, Revenue, Retainers, War, Works and Justice - found at every level from the Empire down to the province, where they carry out the policy the chancellery sets.

girder.def: The main beam of a bridge, which carries the deck and rests at each end on the abutment.

footing.def: The slab or timber pad spread under a bridge's abutment that carries its weight into the ground; a strip footing is a shallow one laid in a band rather than sunk deep.

stringer.def: A lengthwise beam running from abutment to abutment that carries the decking; in a timber bridge, a whole or sawn log.

superstructure.def: Everything a bridge carries above its supports - beams, decking and rail - as opposed to the abutments and footings beneath.

backwall.def: The upright face at the back of an abutment that holds the roadway fill from spilling onto the beam's seat.

wingwall.def: A short wall angling back from an abutment, holding the embankment fill at a bridge's end from sliding sideways.

footplank.def: A single plank laid across a narrow watercourse for those on foot, resting on the banks with no abutment under it.

embankment.def: A raised bank of earth - the one a roadway runs on where it approaches a bridge, or the one that holds water back.

NRCS.def: The US Natural Resources Conservation Service, whose technical supplements govern the design of small rural bridges.

shoulder month.def: The harvest month at the end of the growing season, when the sun stands low - about 28 degrees at 9am and 3pm at 38N - while the grain is being threshed and the autumn greens are still in the ground; its long shadows set how much clear ground a yard or bed needs.

threshing yard.def: The flat, open, sunlit yard beside a farmhouse where the harvested grain was threshed; the record keeps 39 ft of clear ground south of it.

enoki.def: Japanese hackberry, a tall, broad-crowned deciduous tree, one of the trees of a Tonami homestead grove.

sun lane.def: A strip of ground kept clear of trees beside a yard or garden bed so a grove's shadow cannot reach it; here, 50 ft west and southwest of every yard and bed.

ujigami.def: A guardian god of a household or lineage; at a farmstead, one of the gods kept in the corner shrine as the homestead's protector.

Hyakusho Denki.def: A Japanese farming manual of 1681, quoted on rotting night soil in a storage jar before it goes on the fields.

Nogyo Zensho.def: A Japanese farming book published in 1697, which advises letting dung lie and rot until ripe before it is used.

soffit.def: The underside of an overhanging eave; firewood stacked beneath one stays out of the rain.

cutbank.def: The steep outer bank of a stream's bend, where the current cuts into the land.

jitter.def: Varied at random within a set range, so that repeated features such as tree crowns are not all drawn at one size or spacing.

longan.def: A south Chinese evergreen fruit tree, related to the litchi, with small round brown-skinned fruit.

monospecific.def: Made up of a single species; a bamboo stand is one clone, with little else growing in it.

qi.def: In fengshui, the vital energy believed to flow through land, wind and water; a grove at the water mouth was held to keep evil qi out.

rhizome.def: The underground stem a bamboo spreads by; new shoots come up from it, so a stand is one plant creeping outward.

sasa.def: Dwarf bamboo, or bamboo grass, under 2 m tall, common on and near ridgelines; Japan's topographic maps give it a symbol of its own, separate from the bamboo grove.

sheath.def: The papery leaf that wraps a young bamboo culm at each joint and is shed as the culm grows; madake's were used to wrap food and to cover geta.

conservation headland.def: A strip along the edge of a crop field managed for wildlife rather than farmed as usual - a modern British practice, introduced in the 1980s.

crop margin.def: The band 6 ft wide along a field's edge that the map keeps free of scrub, because the grass beside a crop was kept cut.

crown shyness.def: The gap many tree species keep between neighboring crowns, so that even a fully stocked canopy does not touch branch to branch.

hardiness zone.def: A North American scale that ranks plants by the coldest winter they survive; zone 7 is a winter low of about 5°F (-15°C).

hydrophilic.def: Water-loving; of plants, those that grow in wet ground at the water's edge, like the vegetation of a natural stream bank.

internode.def: The hollow length of a bamboo culm between two joints; madake's are long, which suits it for weaving baskets and fans.

provincial seat.def: The walled city where a province's governor and offices sit, one rank above a county seat. Xi'an, inside its Ming wall, is the standing example.

dressed stone.def: Stone cut and squared into regular blocks, laid as a wall's footing or face - at Panmen the base of the barbican court's wall, with brick laid above it.

prefectural city.def: The seat of a prefecture, the administrative tier above the county; its walled city ordinarily had more gates than a county seat's - eight against four.

crenellated.def: Of a parapet: notched along its top with regular gaps that defenders shoot through, the solid stretches between them giving cover.

Wujing Zongyao.def: The Northern Song state military compendium of 1044, which prescribes how a city wall, its mamian and their towers are built.

Mozi.def: A Warring States Chinese philosophical text whose later chapters are manuals of city defense.

Shoucheng Lu.def: A Southern Song treatise by Chen Gui on defending a walled city, written from the siege of De'an.

Dongjing Meng Hua Lu.def: Meng Yuanlao's memoir of 1147 recalling life in Kaifeng, the Northern Song capital.

Daxiangguo.def: The great imperially patronized Buddhist monastery in Kaifeng, the Northern Song capital, said at its height to have managed sixty-four departments with several thousand monks.

hereditary temple.def: A Chinese Buddhist temple handed down from master to disciple within one lineage, as against a public monastery, whose abbot was chosen from outside the lineage and which took in any ordained monk.

public monastery.def: A large Chinese Buddhist monastery whose abbot was chosen from outside any one lineage and which took in any ordained monk, as against a hereditary temple.

Chan.def: The Chinese school of Buddhism centered on meditation, known in Japan as Zen.

City God.def: The guardian deity of a walled city, worshipped in an official state cult: each seat of local government had a City God temple, and its highest official led the sacrifices at set times.

liberty.def: A deliberate departure from what history attests, made for the game's sake and stated openly in the record.

Taizu.def: The temple name of the founding emperor of the Ming dynasty, the Hongwu Emperor.

Caishen.def: The Chinese god of wealth, whose image a shop or a household shrine keeps.

Zaojun.def: The Chinese Kitchen God, the household deity of the stove.

wenmiao.def: The Confucian temple attached to a Chinese prefectural or county school, required for every county school by a Tang decree of 630.

Kangxi.def: The reign of the Qing emperor Kangxi (1661-1722); a year is counted within the reign, so Kangxi 9 is 1670.

Shunzhi.def: The reign of the first Qing emperor to rule from Beijing (1644-1661).

five-ring pagoda.def: A Japanese stone memorial pagoda built of five stacked pieces, set over a grave or a mound.

Musashi.def: The old province that Edo stood in; the Musashi gazetteer is its Edo-period local history.

Celestial Order.def: The setting's caste system: samurai, then the half-people (farmers and merchants), then the non-people (laborers, servants and entertainers), with the burakumin lowest. Monks stand outside it.

Shinsei.def: In the setting, the holy figure whose example the monks follow, with one foot in this world and one in the spiritual realm.

holding jail.def: The Edo-period holding prison at Shinagawa; more than seven hundred inmates died in it between 1691 and 1765, and their bodies were buried at a temple nearby.

Chongzhen era.def: The Chongzhen reign of the Ming, 1628 to 1644, the last Ming emperor's; its tenth year is 1637.

department.def: In Ming and Qing China, a department (zhou, 州) was an administrative unit between the prefecture and the county; a departmental school was the government school at its seat.

shinai.def: A practice sword made of bamboo. With protective equipment it made sword training safe enough to spread to commoners.

Tenpo era.def: A Japanese era, 1830 to 1844, when the late-Edo boom in private sword halls began.

anchor culture.def: One of the two historical societies the setting is modeled on: Edo-period Japan and late imperial China.

hitoyado.def: A placement broker of the early modern cities, which supplied wage-earning servants from peasant and townsman households on one-year, half-year or day terms to samurai households with no connections of their own to find them. The trade grew up with the cities.

hiyoza.def: A channel of hire for day laborers, named beside the hitoyado placement brokers as a route by which peasants and townsmen entered wage service in samurai households.

wakato.def: A young foot-retainer of a samurai household, the lowest of its armed attendants of samurai standing, ranked just above the chugen and, like them, wearing a single sword.

yoriai-seki.def: A senior seat among a domain's retainers, held by old families with large fiefs, such as the Suganuma of Fukui.

onari-goten.def: The reception hall of a great house, kept for a visit by the lord.

intramural.def: Inside the walls - the ground a town's wall encloses, as against the suburbs and estates that stand outside it.

rampart.def: The defensive earth-and-stone wall around a city, thick enough to be drawn as a band rather than a line.

trunk street.def: A town's main street, the one that runs between its gates and that the lesser streets branch off. The standard Chinese plans laid out trunk streets as a cross or a T, and most surviving plans bend them so that none runs straight from one gate to the opposite one.

kotaiyoriai.def: A bannerman (hatamoto) house of high rank that held its own land and, like a daimyo, made the alternate attendance to Edo, though its stipend was below a daimyo's.

jishinban.def: A town ward's own watch house in an Edo-period city, kept by the townspeople: from it the neighborhood was patrolled and the fire watch kept, and its ladder, alarm bell and firefighting gear stood there.

town magistrate.def: In Edo, the shogunate's official over the townsmen's quarters; the machi-bikeshi fire companies were placed under the town magistrate's command.

kidoban.def: The watchman the townsmen of Edo kept at the ward gate (kido) on a machi's boundary.

zongjia.def: In Ming China, the headman of the lowest level of local government, in charge of fire and theft; the posts' heads and firemen of a county town worked under him.

pu.def: In Ming China, a post: a small neighborhood unit of a town, with a head and three to five firemen who took turns keeping the night watch against fire and theft.

fang.def: A ward of a Chinese city: one of the neighborhood units a town was divided into, each holding several posts of the night watch.

micro-high.def: A patch of ground only slightly higher than the plain around it, dry enough that paddy water cannot reach it, so it takes dry fields or houses.

Ishikawa method.def: A Meiji-era way of consolidating paddy land: every parcel is squared into a rectangle that abuts both a branch road and a supply-and-drainage channel.

geostrophic.def: Of the wind high above the ground, beyond the drag of the land or water beneath it; the wind near the surface is slowed from it, over rough land by 40% to 50% and over open water by only 20% to 30%.

reeling.def: Unwinding the silk thread from cocoons softened in boiling water: the old machine was a furnace to boil the water, a wheel to collect the combined thread, and an axle worked by a foot treadle.

header reservoir.def: A storage pond at the upstream head of a water system, from which the channels below it are fed.

rick.def: A stack of straw built in the open after threshing, kept for fodder, fuel or thatch.

wet run.def: The two fenced parts of a fish-cum-duck pond: the dry run is a fenced stretch of the pond dike, and the wet run is a corner of the water fenced off for the ducks.

Kuwabata.def: The project's example dike-pond hamlet: a silk-and-fish hamlet whose mulberry-planted dikes ring fish ponds, with its houses on the dry flank.

Inashiro.def: The project's example rice (paddy) hamlet, the one the dike-pond hamlet is measured against.

rent bursary.def: An office through which Lower Yangzi landlords living in town collected rent from their tenant villages, often backed by the county government.

horinouchi.def: The seat of a medieval Japanese resident lord, named for the moat (hori) and the bank of piled earth (doi) that usually ran around it; it stood on its own fields, with storehouses, stables and servants' huts inside.

gōshi.def: A rural samurai of the Edo period who kept living on and farming their own land instead of moving to the castle town; Kōchi domain's are the best known.

middle moat.def: In a castle town, the ring of moat between the castle's own moat and the outer edge of the town; upper samurai built their residences inside it, and lower samurai lived around its outer edge.

kui.def: The mallow, grown in early China as a leaf vegetable; the Qimin yaoshu's chapter on planting it is where the treatise sets out its garden beds and its market garden.

commandery.def: In early imperial China, a large administrative district above the county, governed from a walled seat; the treatise names its towns as the markets a commercial garden served.

stream order.def: A stream's rank in its river network: the smallest headwater streams are first order, and where two streams of the same order meet, the stream below them is one order higher.

kaya.def: Thatching grass: the tall grasses a village cut every year from its kayaba, a stretch of grassland near the settlement that was burned each year to keep forest from taking hold.

Kinai.def: The capital region of old Japan around Kyoto and Nara, including Osaka and the Yodo river basin; the home provinces.

Ieyasu.def: Tokugawa Ieyasu, the first Tokugawa shogun, who made Edo his seat; his son Hidetada was the second shogun.

reach.def: A stretch of a river between two points, such as two bends, bridges or confluences. Pre-modern river names often belonged to one reach rather than to the whole river.

main stem.def: The principal channel of a river system, the one its tributaries and branches flow into.

floodway.def: A channel dug to carry a river's flood water around a city or low ground, as the Arakawa floodway takes the Arakawa's floods away from Edo's old channel.

Daijokan.def: The Council of State, the highest administrative body of the classical Japanese court, whose edicts carried the court's orders.

rakugo.def: Japanese comic storytelling: one seated performer tells a long story, playing every character.

kana.def: The Japanese syllabic script, in which each sign stands for one syllable; の, read "no", is one of its signs.

mizugaki.def: Another name for the tamagaki, a shrine's fence; at a great shrine with several rings, the innermost.

shimenawa.def: The twisted straw rope hung to mark something sacred, such as a shrine's sacred tree.

ōiya.def: A covering building put over a small shrine sanctuary to shelter it from wind and rain.

chikaraishi.def: A strength stone: a heavy river stone kept beside a shrine's approach and lifted by young men in trials of strength.

sonsha.def: The village-shrine rank in Japan's modern shrine registers: a village's own tutelary shrine, one step above the unranked.

mukakusha.def: An unranked shrine in Japan's modern shrine registers, often a single hamlet's, one step below a village shrine.

ichi-no-torii.def: The first torii of a shrine's approach, usually its largest, standing where the approach enters the grounds; the second and third (ni-no-torii, san-no-torii) stand farther in, toward the hall.

Hachiman.def: A Shinto god of war and archery, patron of warriors, whose shrines are among the commonest in Japan.

irimoya.def: A hip-and-gable roof: hipped on its lower slopes, with a small gable at each end of the ridge.

nagare-zukuri.def: The flowing-roof style of shrine sanctuary, its front roof slope carried out long over the steps; the commonest form of honden in Japan.

dashigeta.def: An eave construction in which a beam carried on projecting joist-ends, set out past the wall face, supports the rafters so the eave reaches farther.

sakaki.def: An evergreen shrub of the tea family whose leafy branches are offered at Shinto shrines, and which is planted in precincts as a sacred tree.

dohyō.def: The ring sumo is wrestled in: a raised square platform of packed clay with a circle of straw bales on top, consecrated by a rite before the bouts.

undersluice.def: At a river headworks, the gated low part of the weir beside the canal's intake: the silt-laden bottom water is passed on downstream through it, so that the cleaner top water is what feeds the canal.

separation zone.def: Where a side channel enters another, the pocket inside the junction where the flow breaks away from the bank and eddies instead of running on; the wider the junction angle, the larger it grows.

Five Highways.def: The five trunk roads of Edo-period Japan, the Tokaido among them. Their ordinary width was about 3 to 4 ken (5.4 to 7.2 m), wider close to Edo, and carts were forbidden on them until the Meiji period.

post-horse system.def: The relay of horses kept along the highways to carry goods and travelers from one stage to the next. The shogunate banned carts from the highways so that the relay would not run short of horses.

footslope.def: The gentle lower slope at the foot of a hill or fan, above the wet ground. Here it is the dry ground a track can use to pass the ends of the wet toe.

fudoki.def: A gazetteer - an official record of a province's villages, roads and landmarks; the Shinpen Musashi fudoki ko, compiled in 1830, is the one for Musashi province.

pledged land.def: Farmland handed to a lender as security for a loan; the lender held or worked it until the loan was repaid, and kept it if the loan was not.

coursing.def: In masonry, the laying of stone in level horizontal rows (courses); a coursing line is the joint running along between two rows.

hiro.def: A Japanese length of about 1.8 m (six shaku), the span of outstretched arms; used for the lengths of boats and rope.

donggusup.def: A Korean village-entrance grove: the stand of trees kept at the mouth of a village, the Korean counterpart of the Chinese water-mouth grove.

hydrosere.def: The zonation from open water to dry land that every lowland wetland shows: open water, then the shallows, then reed swamp, then a sedge and wet-meadow zone, then dry ground.

Baidu Baike.def: A Chinese online encyclopedia whose entries anyone may edit; the record cites it only as an encyclopedia summary, not as a primary text.

bastion.def: A spur of masonry projecting from the outer face of a city wall, from which archers can shoot along the wall to either side; on a Chinese wall, the mamian.

menbansho.def: The main guard house of a Japanese barrier station, holding the upper guard office, a rest room and a bath.

mukaibansho.def: The second guard house of a Japanese barrier station, standing across from the main one, with the station's jail.

gogura.def: The village store for the tax rice in Edo-period Japan: one to a village or to several, holding the rice on its way out under strict guard.

myoji-taito.def: The privilege of bearing a surname and wearing a sword: a warrior privilege that the domains at times granted to commoners too, such as country samurai, headmen of special pedigree and town elders.

Wanshu zaji.def: A Ming-dynasty record of Wanping county, the county town in Beijing, quoted in the record for the town's fire-and-theft wards and watch posts.

yokocho.def: A side street off a main street: narrower than the main street but wider and more public than a roji back lane.

kirisute-gomen.def: A warrior's privilege in Edo-period Japan, named beside myoji-taito: the license to cut down a commoner who gave offense.

keibodan.def: Japan's wartime civil-defense guard, a modern body; the record names it only to show that the night fire round it walked is not dated to the Edo period.

shobodan.def: Japan's volunteer fire brigade, a modern local body that still walks the night fire round.

jobikeshi.def: The shogunate's own standing fire watch of Edo, organized after the Meireki fire of 1657, with fire-brigade mansions and fire towers at several places in the castle town.

jinaicho.def: A Japanese temple town ringed by a moat and rampart, the closed counterpart of the open gate-front town.

tauchiguruma.def: A hand-pushed weeder run between the rows of a paddy, promoted with rope-and-ruler row planting in Meiji-era Japan.

yui.def: Exchanged labor between farm households, lending one another hands at transplanting; it works because the households' planting dates differ.

oyaike.def: Parent pond: the chief pond of a Japanese parent-child system of irrigation ponds, with smaller child ponds (koike) grouped under it.

koike.def: Child pond: one of the smaller irrigation ponds grouped under a parent pond (oyaike) in a Japanese parent-child pond system.

weineihe.def: The inner ring canal of a Chinese polder, running just inside the dike and feeding the field ditches.

adlittoral.def: Of a water plant, grown in the shallows at the water's edge; adlittoral lotus varieties stand in 10 to 20 cm of water.

kumi-chi.def: Ground assigned to one unit of foot soldiers, where the men of that unit lived together.

An'ei.def: A Japanese era name: the years 1772 to 1781.

Bunsei.def: The Japanese era 1818 to 1830, when the three great sword schools of Edo were opened.

Kanbun.def: A Japanese era name: the years 1661 to 1673.

Jokyo.def: The Japanese era 1684 to 1688, of the halving of retainers' fiefs the record quotes.

wicket.def: A small door set in a larger gate, let open for one person at a time while the gate itself stays shut.

junk.def: The Chinese cargo sailing boat that carried bulk goods on river and canal.

raku.def: A low-fired, hand-formed Japanese pottery, taken from the kiln hot and simply glazed.

murabarai.def: Banishment from the village: the heaviest punishment a village could put on one of its own.

tokorobarai.def: Banishment from one's place of residence, the punishment the record names beside murabarai.

Wubei Zhi.def: A great Ming-dynasty military treatise (1621), quoted in the record for what a wall's bastions were for.

normal depth.def: The depth at which water in a channel flows steadily and evenly, the level a river settles back to some way upstream of a gate or weir.

笞.def: The light bamboo cane, the lightest of the Five Punishments of the Chinese legal code: a beating on the buttocks, given in court by the yamen's runners.

杖.def: The heavy stick, the second of the Five Punishments of the Chinese legal code: a beating with a large stick on the back, buttocks or legs, given in court by the yamen's runners.

pit rank.def: The row of soaking pits in a tanning yard, where hides lie in the tanning liquor. It runs along the yard's edge of water, and the number of pits sets the yard's size.

staking frame.def: A frame set in the shallows at a tanning yard's bank, where salted hides are held in the river to steep for several days before the hair is scraped off.

settlement core.def: The middle of a settlement's dwellings, the point from which a direction out of town is measured.

night watch.def: One of the five periods the night was divided into, from dusk to dawn. The drum and bell tower sounded each one, and watchmen carried it through the streets with clappers and gongs.

hour of xu.def: The eleventh of the twelve two-hour periods of the traditional Chinese day, about 7 to 9 in the evening. The drum and bell towers struck it to open the night.

plinth.def: The block or low stone base that a pillar, post or wall stands on, keeping the timber or earth above it off the wet ground.

city grain.def: The scale a city map is drawn at, about 3 ft of ground to a pixel, where a mark must be about 6 ft across to be seen at all.

picket line.def: A rope stretched between stakes or posts, with several animals tied along it in a row.

stele.def: An upright stone slab or post, often carved or inscribed; the Chinese hitching post counts as one.

ever-normal granary.def: A Chinese state granary that bought grain when it was cheap and sold it when it was dear, to keep the price steady and hold a reserve against famine.

Qianlong.def: The reign of the Qing emperor Qianlong, 1736-1796.

Jiaqing.def: The reign of the Qing emperor Jiaqing, 1796-1820.

Azuchi-Momoyama period.def: The years from about 1568 to 1600, between the Sengoku period and the Edo period, when Japan was reunified and firearms came into wide use; castle walls were thickened against bullets.

loophole.def: A narrow opening cut through a castle wall so that defenders can shoot out through it.

formwork.def: The temporary boards that hold earth or plaster in shape while a wall is rammed or set; they are taken away once the wall stands.

commutation.def: Paying a tax owed in one thing - rice, in this record - in another, usually coin, at a reckoned rate.

kokudai-no.def: Paying the land tax, or a share of it, in money reckoned at the price of the rice owed; one Edo source puts it at three to four tenths of the whole tax.

natto.def: A Japanese food of soybeans fermented until sticky.

randori.def: Free practice in jujutsu and the other grappling arts: partners attack and throw each other freely rather than following a set sequence. It needs a floor that can take a fall, which is one reason practice halls came to be floored with boards or tatami.

Four Books and Five Classics.def: The core Confucian texts that a domain school's pupils recited, starting at age seven or eight and before they took up the martial arts. They are the Chinese canon that samurai learned their letters from.

enfeoffment.def: A lord's grant of a domain to a vassal, who holds it in return for service - as when Ikeda Terumasa was granted Himeji in 1600 at an assessed yield of 520,000 koku.

kuruwa.def: The Japanese word for a castle's bailey: one of the walled or ditched enclosures a castle's layout divides its ground into, the innermost being the honmaru.

shell keep.def: A castle's strongest tower is its keep, its last refuge; a shell keep is a ring wall built around the top of a castle mound in place of that tower, and a square keep is the older four-cornered tower whose corners were its weak points.

trebuchet.def: A siege engine that throws stones from a pivoting beam, worked by a counterweight or by a crew hauling ropes; in Europe it came into use around the end of the 12th century.

dead ground.def: Ground at the foot of a wall that its defenders cannot shoot into from the wall-top; at a square corner, the angle itself.

siege mining.def: Digging a tunnel (a gallery) under a wall, propping it with timber, then burning the props so the wall above collapses; a square corner was the miner's favorite target.

Hakka.def: A Han Chinese group of the hill country where Fujian, Guangdong and Jiangxi meet, whose clans built most of the Fujian tulou.

Suzaku-oji.def: The great central avenue of an ancient Chinese-model imperial capital, running south from the palace gate: 82-84 m wide at Heian-kyo and 147 m at Tang Chang'an (Zhuque Dajie).

Heian-kyo.def: The ancient imperial capital at present-day Kyoto, founded in 794 and laid out as a grid on the Chinese model.

Heijo-kyo.def: The imperial capital at Nara before Heian-kyo, also a grid on the Chinese model.

Engishiki.def: A 10th-century collection of Japanese court procedures and regulations, completed in 927, which records the dimensions of Heian-kyo.

Bunka.def: The Japanese era name for the years 1804-1818, in the late Edo period.

Morisada manko.def: A late-Edo-period survey of the customs and daily life of Edo, Kyoto and Osaka, compiled by Kitagawa Morisada.

yamen-god.def: The god of the government office itself, whose small temple a Chinese county yamen kept inside its walls beside the earth-god shrine.

jail-god.def: The deity of a Chinese yamen's jail, enshrined in a small temple inside the jail itself; at Neixiang the statue is of the ancient judge Gao Yao.

Dacheng gate.def: The gate before the main hall of a Chinese Confucian temple; the shrines to meritorious local officials and to local worthies stood outside it, one on each side.

Important Cultural Property.def: Japan's national designation for a single building or object protected for its historic value; Shibata's foot-soldier row house is one.

Dading.def: A twelfth-century Chinese reign era (the name of an emperor's years) of the Jin dynasty in north China; its third year was 1163.

GM.def: The game master: the person running the campaign these maps are drawn for, whose questions and rulings this record answers.

remand.def: Holding an accused person in custody until their case is judged, as opposed to confinement as a sentence; the ordinary work of an Edo-period jail.

gokumon.def: An Edo-period death sentence carried out by beheading, one of the three grades the Tenmachō jail article names beside shizai and geshunin.

geshunin.def: An Edo-period death sentence carried out by beheading, one of the three grades the Tenmachō jail article names beside gokumon and shizai.

yotsu.def: "Four": the Edo-period name for the night hour around 10 pm (the hours were counted down from nine). After it, a town block's kido were shut and anyone with business went through the wicket past the watchman.

wallow.def: A mud pond or pool where water buffalo lie to keep cool in hot weather; they need one as well as a trough.

well-house.def: A small roofed shelter built over the mouth of a well; on these maps, the roof square drawn over a wellhead.

Enokida.def: One of the project's sample maps: a village whose paddy is laid out as a polder, where every low plot wears the wet-paddy tint.

dissection.def: The cutting of a plateau or upland into valleys by the streams that erode it.

unhair.def: In tanning, to strip the hair from a hide; in shironameshi the salted hides are first soaked in the river for several days to loosen it.

eta.def: The hereditary outcaste status of pre-Meiji Japan, whose members disposed of fallen cattle and horses, worked hides and leather, and served as executioners, constables and watchmen; in eastern Japan they were governed through the head Danzaemon.

buraku.def: An outcaste settlement; each had its own head, who guarded it and was paid by its residents.

gross-up.def: The factor by which a dwelling's drawn footprint is multiplied to give the ground it costs a city: the footprint plus its share of eaves, lanes and street margins.

budget model.def: The project's reckoning of the ground a city's households, castle and public buildings need, from which the size and circuit of its wall are derived.

reform and opening-up.def: China's turn to market economics and foreign trade from the end of the 1970s; the record uses it to date the modern commercialization that widened the Pearl delta's ponds and narrowed their dikes.

Shunde.def: A county, now a district, of the Pearl delta south of Guangzhou, at the heart of the dike-pond country; mulberry dominated its dikes from the late Ming.

Kanto.def: The plain around Edo in eastern Japan, where the shogunate held much of its own land and its intendants lived in Edo rather than in the villages they governed.

house pad.def: A raised platform of packed earth that a house is built on, lifting it above the surrounding ground and flood water.

tax-farming.def: Handing a tax's collection to agents who profit from what they gather; here, the permanent clerks' chance to enrich themselves out of the revenue that passes through their hands.

Hayakawa.def: One of the two example county manors drawn for this project, beside Ochiba: a magistracy compound of about 247 by 200 ft, with a tally office at its river landing.

draw-basin.def: A basin inside the city wall where residents drew the aqueduct's water from the buried pipes - what a resident sees of the supply, beside the wells.

hokaku sen.def: The grid lines of the jori land system, which divide one square of farmland from the next. They generally run north-south and east-west, but in a fair number of regions the whole grid is tilted.

Dujiangyan.def: The ancient irrigation works on the Min River in Sichuan, whose canals fan out across the Chengdu plain below the diversion.

caoshi.def: A commercial district that grew up outside a Chinese city's walls, beginning in the Song dynasty. It descends from the rural periodic market of the Tang.

ward-and-market system.def: The Tang city's order in which residents lived in walled wards whose gates the street drum opened at sunrise and closed at sunset, and trade was held in designated markets.

periodic market.def: A market held on fixed days of a recurring cycle rather than every day - in Japan the rokusai-ichi met six times a month - to which the peasants of the surrounding countryside came in to buy and sell.

Manji.def: A Japanese era name of the early Edo period; its first year, Manji 1, is 1658.

Chang'an.def: The capital of the Tang dynasty: a walled city laid out in walled wards whose gates were shut at the dusk drum.

Yasuki Taka.def: The first Imperial Treasurer in the setting, whose system separates the official who assesses what is owed from the one who collects it; the import tariff collected at provincial-city and capital gates follows it.

at grade.def: On the same level: two channels, or a channel and a road, that cross at grade meet on one surface rather than one passing over the other, so their water or traffic mixes where they cross.

omotedana.def: A shop-house facing a main street, whose master was often landlord of the back-street tenements behind it (uradana, ura-nagaya).

Imperial spine.def: The Imperial highway where it runs through a city as its main street; a river city has none, since its highway passes off the map instead.

DEM.def: Digital elevation model: a map of ground heights laid out as a grid of cells, here 90 meters on a side.

SRTM.def: Shuttle Radar Topography Mission: the radar survey flown on a space shuttle in 2000, whose height data covers most of the Earth's land.

sand junk.def: A flat-bottomed Chinese wooden cargo sailing ship (shachuan), built for the shallow, sandy waters around the Yangtze mouth and the northern coast.

dispersed settlement.def: A countryside where each farmhouse stands apart among its own fields instead of gathered in a cluster, as on Japan's Tonami Plain, where farmers built amid their rice fields to manage their water; the opposite of a nucleated settlement.

gōsha.def: The district-shrine rank in Japan's modern shrine registers: the chief shrine of a district of about twenty villages, one step above the village shrine.

sōchinju.def: A castle town's principal tutelary shrine, guarding the whole town rather than one quarter or village; Edo's was the Sannō shrine.

preceptor.def: A cleric of one of the setting's Orders; every town has one preceptor per Order, and a town preceptor serves in a town monastery, where the Order's monks live under them.

Sōtō.def: A school of Zen Buddhism; the temples of the Hiki register quoted here and the Aichi training temple with its meditation hall and monks' dormitory are Sōtō.

Tendai.def: A school of Japanese Buddhism; several of the Hiki district temples quoted in the record, Anyōji among them, are Tendai.

Martial temple.def: In a Chinese walled city, the temple to the god of war, set opposite the Confucian temple across the main street, as at Pingyao.

jōgōe-chi.def: One of the ranks of a Sōtō temple, with the kata-hōdōe-chi and the zuiie-chi, at which the ninety-day training retreat was held in the Edo period and a full set of halls was required.

Chinese-style gate.def: A Japanese gate type named for its Chinese-style roof (a curved, cusped gable), not a gate built in China. It marked a shrine or temple of some standing; Sano's district shrine Asahimori had one.

adept.def: In this setting, a monk of the rank that may marry and raise children. A married adept's family lives in an ordinary home near the temple.

initiate.def: In this setting, a lay person studying religion under a temple while working an ordinary job. A temple has about twice as many initiates as monks, and only a few of them sleep inside its walls.

tsujido.def: A small open wayside hall on four corner posts under a tiled roof, with a board floor about two mats in size, built by a settlement beside a road for travelers to rest and later housing a jizo or other stone image.

koshin tower.def: A roadside stone of the koshin cult, one of the stones that stand together at the entrance to a village beside its dosojin.
